reviews.text: The hand-painted city and dense side streets make exploration rewarding. Brief frame-time spikes interrupt otherwise smooth movement.
Weapons support genuinely different combat styles, and enemy groups ask the player to switch tactics. The camera becomes unreliable in tight rooms.
Environmental storytelling and the restrained score create a memorable atmosphere. Several optional errands repeat the same objective.
Combat inputs feel responsive and boss patterns are readable. Late chapters reuse too many minibosses.
Art direction and sound design remain striking throughout. Shader stutter is still visible on PC during new-area traversal.

supported_dislike_themes: repetitive optional content or reused enemies

reviews.text: Co-op is the most fun I have had with friends this year, but our sessions disconnect several times each evening.
The character builder offers lots of viable combinations. The tutorial explains status effects poorly.
Finding hidden rooms feels rewarding, although moving items between storage tabs takes too many steps.
Controls are precise and dodging feels consistent. Matchmaking frequently fails before a co-op session starts.
There is a generous amount of content for a first playthrough. The opening hours introduce too many systems at once.
The soundtrack is excellent, but the interface text is uncomfortably small on a television.
The central mystery is carefully foreshadowed, and the lead performances give its quieter scenes real weight.
Expressive lighting and strong composition make even ordinary conversations visually distinctive. The middle act moves too slowly.
The supporting cast is convincingly performed, but repeated exposition weakens the pacing.
Its final narrative turn follows logically from earlier clues. Facial animation sometimes distracts from emotional scenes.
Aiming feels immediate on a controller, and restarts load quickly after a failed round.
Local co-op works well, but online matchmaking often leaves me waiting without finding a lobby.
Movement is responsive and remapping is flexible. Cosmetic bundles cost far too much.
Loading is fast on console. Two of my three online sessions ended when the host connection dropped.
Playing on the same couch is excellent, while the rotating store makes basic outfits feel overpriced.
The high difficulty made every victory satisfying, and failures usually taught me what to change.
Difficulty spikes arrive without warning, so I stopped enjoying the campaign halfway through.
Boss attacks are clearly signaled and learning them feels fair.
Repeating long sections after a mistake makes the challenge exhausting rather than rewarding.
I liked mastering demanding encounters because the rules stayed consistent.
The camera hides attacks during two bosses, which makes those fights feel unfair.

The campaign regularly changes its objectives: a defensive hold becomes an evacuation, while a later investigation turns into a chase. These transitions keep familiar locations interesting. The inventory, however, hides frequently used tools inside several nested categories.
Optional missions offer meaningful routes instead of simply repeating the campaign. Crowded hub areas show uneven frame pacing, especially when several vendors and effects appear together.

Sound design communicates danger before the interface does, with distinct cues for nearby machines and incoming attacks. The quest log groups unrelated objectives together and makes the next step difficult to locate.
Main missions combine traversal, negotiation, and combat in varied proportions. Performance drops are noticeable during large outdoor battles but do not appear in smaller interiors.
The orchestral score adapts cleanly when a quiet search becomes a confrontation. Managing equipment is slower than necessary because comparison details disappear when switching tabs.
Several strong missions allow objectives to be completed in a different order, and characters respond to that choice. Dense particle effects cause short frame-rate drops on the tested console.
Audio cues remain precise even when the screen is busy, and ambient sound gives each district a distinct identity. Menu navigation requires too many confirmations for routine crafting.
The best side missions introduce mechanics that later reappear in the main path, so they feel connected rather than disposable. The map legend is clear, but the quest list itself is poorly organized.
Objective variety sustains the campaign across its substantial length. A few set pieces briefly stutter when streaming a new district, which weakens otherwise impressive transitions.
Voice direction is consistently strong and helps minor characters feel specific. I found the final scene emotionally weak, although this issue does not recur elsewhere.
